name: Eflornithine (Vaniqa)

lead: Eflornithine cream (Vaniqa, 13.9 percent) is an FDA-approved prescription treatment for unwanted facial hair in women, approved in December 2000. It slows regrowth so facial hair is less visible between shaving or plucking sessions.

It irreversibly inhibits ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme needed for polyamine production and cell growth, which slows the growth of new hair in follicles without destroying them. In the two vehicle-controlled trials behind its approval, more women improved on the cream than on vehicle, though many showed only partial improvement. It is not hair removal.

paras: Women apply it to the affected facial area as a prescribed routine, alongside shaving, plucking or light-based hair reduction rather than instead of them. Hair returns to its previous rate within about eight weeks of stopping.

The most common reported effect is acne, followed by local irritation such as stinging, redness, dryness and itching. It is prescription-only in the US and generally elsewhere. Limited pregnancy data show no clear harm, but interaction studies are lacking.

angle.text: Women use this prescription cream to slow facial hair regrowth so there is less visible hair and less shaving or plucking. It inhibits an enzyme in the follicle, and the effect lasts only while it is used. It is approved for this purpose.

lead: Eflornithine, also known as difluoromethylornithine (DFMO), is an inhibitor of the enzyme ornithine decarboxylase. Its 13.9 percent topical cream, sold as Vaniqa, is a prescription product approved in the United States in December 2000 to reduce unwanted facial hair in women [1][2]. Systemic forms of the same molecule are used for other conditions, including second-stage African sleeping sickness and, since 2023, maintenance therapy in high-risk neuroblastoma [1][3].

Topical eflornithine does not remove hair. Reports describe it as slowing regrowth, with hair returning to its previous rate within about eight weeks of stopping [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and grooming contexts it is mainly relevant to facial and beard-area hair reduction, usually alongside shaving, laser or electrolysis.

paras: Vaniqa is indicated for reducing the severity of unwanted facial hair in women, including the chin area [1][2]. Per the cream's labelling as summarised by Grokipedia, it is applied to the face and used alongside mechanical hair-removal such as shaving or plucking, and visible effects can appear from about 4 to 8 weeks [1].

It has also been studied alongside light-based hair reduction. Grokipedia cites a randomized split-face trial in women with facial hirsutism in which the cream prolonged the hair reduction achieved with intense pulsed light [1]. A phase 4 trial registered in 2025 compares a face cream plus a laser procedure with face cream alone for excess facial hair in women [4].

Eflornithine given by injection is used with nifurtimox against second-stage Trypanosoma brucei gambiense sleeping sickness, and a randomized phase III trial found the combination non-inferior to eflornithine alone [3]. In December 2023 the US FDA approved oral eflornithine (Iwilfin) as maintenance therapy to reduce relapse risk in high-risk neuroblastoma [1][5]. These uses are unrelated to hair.

Grokipedia summarises two vehicle-controlled trials of 594 women with moderate to severe facial hirsutism treated for 24 weeks. In the pooled data, 58 percent of women on eflornithine showed at least some improvement against 34 percent on vehicle, and about 32 percent showed marked improvement or better against 8 percent [1]. Wikipedia reports that 81 percent of women showed clinical improvement after 12 months in studies, with early results at about eight weeks [2].

Both sources say the effect depends on continued use: regrowth returns to baseline within roughly eight weeks after stopping, and the cream is not a depilatory [1][2]. Subgroup results in the label data differed by group, and the benefit is described as partial slowing of growth rather than elimination [1]. Some trials also reported reductions in the psychological burden of facial hair [1][2].

Wikipedia reports acne as the most frequent adverse effect of the cream (about 7 to 14 percent), with irritation reactions such as burning, stinging, dryness, itching, redness, rash and ingrown-hair reactions each reported in more than 1 percent of users [2]. Limited data from pregnancies exposed to the topical form showed no clinical evidence of harm, although interaction studies have not been done [2].

Eflornithine is a structural analogue of ornithine that irreversibly inhibits ornithine decarboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in polyamine synthesis, which supports cell growth and division [1][2]. In hair follicles this is the proposed route by which the cream slows growth of new hair [1].

Merrell Dow developed eflornithine in the late 1970s as a cancer drug; it was ineffective against malignancies but was found to affect hair growth and parasites [2]. The injectable form Ornidyl was approved in the US in 1990 for sleeping sickness, and Grokipedia reports that production was sustained after near discontinuation through the 2000 approval of the topical cream and WHO-brokered donations from the manufacturer from 2001 [1][2].
Vaniqa is prescription-only in the US and generally elsewhere [2]. The available sources contain no sourced looksmaxxing-forum discussion, so its use in those communities is not documented here.

Two vehicle-controlled multicentre trials of topical 13.9 percent eflornithine in 594 women with facial hirsutism form the basis of the US approval, with the response rates described under Effectiveness [1]. A randomized split-face study combined it with intense pulsed light [1], and a 2025 phase 4 trial of cream plus laser versus cream alone in 122 women is recruiting [4]. A randomized trial of topical eflornithine for pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps) was terminated after enrolling nine participants [6]. Large randomized trials of systemic eflornithine concern sleeping sickness, where nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy was found non-inferior [3], and cancer settings [5].
